source.title: Harmful Intent as a Geometrically Recoverable Feature of LLM Residual Streams

record.tranche_reason: The study refines the single-direction account: its own results show that harmful-intent detection is concentrated within an extraction protocol but that different protocols can recover substantially different directions. It also tests whether detection transfers across model variants and persists in abliterated variants.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-versus-benign detection and direction geometry, not refusal or compliance generation. It projects directions out of cached activations and evaluates detection; it does not ablate all layers and positions in the model, add a direction to induce refusal, or test whether attacks suppress refusal. Its comparisons with refusal behavior and the Zhao et al. results are discussion of cited work, not results from this study.
record.test_reason: Only V5 is tested. Harm-vs-benign detection stays near-ceiling in four community-abliterated checkpoints, where the refusal direction was removed by weight orthogonalisation. That is a probe-based test of whether harm recognition is encoded apart from the refusal mechanism. All other results measure the geometry and transfer of harm-detection directions, not refusal. No refusal rates are measured, no direction is ablated or added in the forward pass, and the lt/chat direction is never shown to mediate refusal. So V1, V4, V6 and V7 are not tested for refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that harmful intent is linearly recoverable across 12 models (and up to 9B in Qwen3.5) and persists in abliterated variants. They read this as corroborating Zhao et al.'s harm/refusal dissociation. The recovered direction is concentrated within each extraction protocol but protocol-dependent across them, so probing does not isolate a unique computational feature. They add that AUROC masks low-FPR variation, so operating-point metrics should be reported.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits directions to classify harmful versus benign prompts and evaluates AUROC/TPR; it does not reproduce the original refusal-generation ablation or harmless-prompt steering intervention. Its projection experiments remove directions from cached activations and refit detectors, rather than removing a direction from every model layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Extraction protocol changes the direction and projection outcome: max-pool versus last-token, raw versus chat-templated input. Layer selection is protocol-specific; the paper also reports a Qwen2.5 middle-layer valley for projection-based detection. Alignment changes transfer in Gemma-3 much more than in the other tested families.

fits_no_version.finding: Harm-detection directions from max-pool and last-token extraction lie about 73° apart. Projecting out the lt/chat (Arditi-style) direction leaves max-pool detection intact but cuts lt/chat detection to 0.60–0.80.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear harm-detection directions are protocol-dependent: different pooling choices recover near-orthogonal directions, each concentrated within its own protocol.

fits_no_version.finding: Base-model harm-detection directions transfer to instruct and abliterated variants within 0.010 AUROC in three families. Gemma-3 rotates 73° and TPR@1%FPR collapses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment can rotate the linear harm-detection direction in some architectures while keeping harmful inputs linearly separable.

record.problems: The study measures detection, not refusal behavior or general capability. Abliterated checkpoints are community-produced, and the paper does not independently verify their refusal behavior. The text's claim that abliterated variants match instruct variants within ±0.003 is inconsistent with the Table 7 wopt values for Qwen2.5 and Qwen3.5 (differences 0.007 and 0.005). The authors also state that the actual computational feature is not identified. Evaluation is single-turn, English, and clean; adversarial, multi-turn, and cross-lingual cases are untested.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. Main detection-performance comparisons among fitting strategies, classifier benchmarks, and cited results from other work were not included because they do not directly test the claim versions' refusal, transfer, or direction-geometry outcomes.

untested.parts: No refusal measurement, ablation, addition or capability check.
Uses abliterated checkpoints but never measures whether they stop refusing.
No refusal-mediating direction is tested; the multi-direction results concern harm detection only.
No behavioural refusal or harm-judgment outputs and no causal steering. Refusal removal in the abliterated models is assumed, not verified.
Transfer is shown only for harm-detection directions, not the refusal direction; no cross-lingual test.
Training procedure and timing are not varied.

missing.what: Instruct-direction to abliterated-variant transfer: Llama 0.988 vs own 0.988, Qwen2.5 0.963 vs 0.961, Qwen3.5 0.985 vs 0.984, Gemma 0.974 vs 0.977. The refusing model's harm direction still works after abliteration.
wLDA instruct vs abliterated AUROC, which differ by up to 0.014 (Qwen2.5 0.975 vs 0.961)
Qwen3.5 2B/4B/9B abliterated-variant detection and transfer, AUROC 0.98–0.99

record.verdict_notes: The record over-links V4, V6 and V7: those rows measure harm-detection probes, not refusal. The lt/chat direction matches Arditi's construction, but the paper validates it only by detection, not by any effect on refusal. Rows r17, r20, r23 and r26 duplicate r8, r10, r12 and r14. The text's ±0.003 abliterated-vs-instruct figure does not match the own-direction Table 7 values; it does match instruct-to-abliterated transfer in Table 15. The V5 verdict rests on assuming the huihui-ai abliterated checkpoints no longer refuse, which the paper does not check.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure refusal after removing the direction from model activations or weights, does not add the direction and measure refusal, and does not assess general capabilities.
Uses community-produced abliterated checkpoints but does not test whether abliteration removes refusal behavior in released models.
No attack suppression of the refusal direction or training against its ablation is tested.

Does not establish the model's computationally used harm-recognition feature; the authors say detection-level probing cannot determine whether protocols recover different views of one feature or distinct features.

Does not independently measure harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions as behavioral outputs or causally manipulate both; persistence of detection in abliterated checkpoints is the evidence reported.
Tests transfer among base, instruction-tuned, and abliterated variants and across model sizes, but not across languages.
Compares alignment variants and direction transfer, but does not vary the refusal-training procedure or when refusal training occurs.

labels.condition: Abliterated vs instruct variants of Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-3-1B, mp/raw probe
labels.reason: Abliterated wopt AUROC is 0.981/0.974/0.991/0.980 vs instruct 0.988/0.979/0.988/0.981 (r1-r4), a gap of at most 0.007. The authors read this as corroborating the harm/refusal dissociation. The evidence is probe-only, and the study does not verify refusal removal.

relation.reason: Its own results (Tables 7-8, 12, 15) bear on whether harm recognition persists without the refusal direction.

tranche.reason: The study probes harm decodability (AUROC of fitted directions) in instruct vs abliterated checkpoints. That differs from Zhao et al.'s causal steering but asks the same V5 question. The authors corroborate the dissociation rather than argue that V5 is wrong or needs restating, so T5 does not fit.

source_check.notes: The paper's headline 'within ±0.003 AUROC' does not match its own Tables 7-8: wopt gaps reach 0.007, and the wLDA gap for Qwen2.5 is 0.975->0.961 (0.014). Further V5-relevant results that r1-r4 do not cover: abliterated Qwen3.5 2B/4B/9B (Table 15), and Appendix G, where refit AUROC stays >=0.949 after the lt/chat refusal direction is projected out of instruct activations.

statements.problem: None for this study. All four instruct->abliterated pairs match Tables 7-8 (wopt, mp/raw, full benign set). All abliterated checkpoints are huihui-ai community releases, and the study does not verify refusal removal. It has bootstrap CIs and controls (random, PC1, perplexity, base variants).
None for this study. Gemma-3-1B wopt mp/raw 0.981 -> 0.980 (Table 8). The checkpoint is huihui-ai/gemma-3-1b-it-abliterated, and its refusal removal is not verified.

statements.correction: Main-set abliterated checkpoints are 0.5B-1.3B (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, Gemma-3-1B). Table 15/Appendix L also evaluates abliterated Qwen3.5 2B, 4B and 9B: own-direction wLDA AUROC, instruct->abliterated, 0.993->0.991, 0.994->0.991, 0.995->0.991 (at the base-selected layer).
statements.problem: Correct that this study reports no behavioural refusal or harm-judgment outputs and assumes refusal removal. But the size bucket '<1B' understates the study's weight-edit coverage.

statements.correction: On chat-templated input, mp vs lt directions are 72.6±6.7 deg apart (at Lmp/chat) and 74.9±9.3 deg (at Llt/chat). Projecting out lt/chat wLDA and refitting changes AUROC by -0.186 to -0.398 under lt/chat, +0.001 to +0.020 under mp/chat and -0.010 to +0.001 under mp/raw (Table 12). Raw->chat under last-token raises mean AUROC 0.972->0.993 and TPR 0.693->0.908 (Table 4).
statements.problem: Pooling (max-pool vs last-token) changes both the direction and the projection outcome. Raw vs chat input does not change the projection outcome, and the text reports no raw-vs-chat direction angle.
Makes no specific claim about this study, and cites no rows from it.
